section_title: FAIR Principles and the Preclinical Data Ecosystem

findings.location: Section 'The declared-versus-actual gap' (para 3) AND figure caption fig-sec4-actual-vs-declared-availability
findings.claim_text: a cross-sectional analysis of oncology articles found that, among datasets declared available, only one - 0.3% - met the remaining FAIR assessment criteria on inspection (Hamilton2022) ... [caption] just 0.3% of datasets declared available met the remaining FAIR criteria ... FAIR-compliant among only those datasets already declared available (Hamilton2022, 0.3%, a stricter conditional bar).
findings.issue: Denominator mismatch (confirmed against the paper's abstract). Hamilton2022 sampled 306 cancer articles; 59/306 (19%) declared data available; the abstract states data met key FAIR principles in 'less than 1% (1/306)'. The 0.3% is therefore 1 of ALL 306 sampled articles, NOT 1 of the 59 declared-available. The prose and the figure caption both attribute 0.3% to the 'declared available' subset and even label it 'a stricter conditional bar' - but 0.3% uses the WIDER (all-sampled) denominator. Computed among the 59 declared-available, the rate would be ~1.7% (1/59), not 0.3%. This is exactly the denominator error the pre-check warned about, and it appears in two places.
findings.evidence: Hamilton2022 abstract: 'One in five studies declared data were publicly available (59/306, 19%)' and '...to less than 1% (1/306, 95% CI: 0-2%) when data were checked for compliance with key FAIR principles.' 1/306 = 0.33%; 1/59 = 1.7%.
findings.suggested_fix: State the denominator correctly, e.g. 'only 1 of 306 sampled oncology articles (0.3%) met the remaining FAIR criteria on inspection' - and drop the 'among datasets declared available'/'stricter conditional bar' framing (or, if the conditional framing is wanted, write '1 of the 59 declared-available datasets, ~1.7%'). Apply the same fix to the figure caption.

findings.location: Section 'Interoperability and ontologies' -> clinical common-data-models paragraph
findings.claim_text: Mapping to the OMOP common data model repeatedly loses domain content: standard OMOP vocabularies could directly represent only a quarter (19 of 75) of core extracorporeal-life-support concepts (Rieder2026), a scoping review found OMOP vocabularies lack the granularity to capture oncology concepts... (Nada2026)...
findings.issue: Suppressed conflict [16]. The section presents OMOP uniformly as content-losing (Rieder2026, Nada2026, Bataille2026, App2026) but omits the package's counter-side, Finster2025, a criteria-based systematic CDM review finding OMOP/OHDSI the largest observational-data network (2.1B records) and one of the best-scoring CDMs. Presenting only the loss side makes OMOP look broadly inadequate rather than dominant-but-lossy-at-the-margins.
findings.evidence: Package conflict [16]: paper_a Finster2025 'found the OMOP/OHDSI network to be the largest observational-data network and FHIR the most widely used interoperability standard'; paper_b Rieder2026 '19 (25%) were directly mappable...'. resolution_status resolved-by-method.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one clause acknowledging OMOP's status, citing Finster2025 (e.g. 'Even the dominant, most-comprehensive observational model, OMOP/OHDSI (Finster2025), repeatedly loses domain content:'), so both sides of the conflict are present.

findings.claim_text: MIAME for microarrays (Brazma2001) seeded a family of checklists - MIAPE for proteomics (Taylor2007)... these are genuine achievements of community consensus. But common data elements ... have not broadly solved interoperability (Kush2020), and community checklists remain ... human-readable narratives ... (Batista2022).
findings.issue: Suppressed conflict [11] (neither side cited). The section discusses MIAPE as a consensus achievement but omits the package's empirical counter-evidence that these proteomics standards fail in practice: Vadadokhau2026, a 2026 reanalysis of six public PRIDE deposits, found missing metadata/proprietary formats produced large reanalysis discrepancies (13,068 vs 4,923 proteins), turning open-access deposits into non-reproducible 'data tombs'. This is primary evidence directly supporting the section's own 'shared is not reusable' thesis. Note: Vadadokhau2026 has a conflict entry but NO finding in the evidence package, so per the hard rule the writer should request a supplementary evidence entry rather than cite from memory.
findings.evidence: Package conflict [11]: paper_b Vadadokhau2026 'these shortcomings yielded large discrepancies in the analysis results (e.g., 13,068 vs. 4,923 proteins...)' vs paper_a MartinezBartolome2013 (MIAPE Quant asserts minimum metadata suffices for reproduction). resolution_status open.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the empirical counter-side near the MIAPE mention (request a supplementary package finding for Vadadokhau2026), e.g. '...yet a 2026 reanalysis of six PRIDE deposits found missing metadata still produced large discrepancies in re-derived protein counts (Vadadokhau2026), leaving standardized deposits as non-reproducible data tombs.'

findings.location: Section 'Interoperability and ontologies: standards without fidelity'
findings.claim_text: Interoperability - the FAIR dimension most dependent on shared ontologies and controlled vocabularies - reveals that adopting a standard does not guarantee faithful data. ... Adherence to an interoperability standard, then, is necessary infrastructure but does not by itself yield complete or faithful data.
findings.issue: Suppressed conflict [7] (neither side cited). The package contains a direct instance of the section's 'standards without fidelity' thesis: Stotl2025 claims ISO/IEC 11179 metadata-registry adoption automatically confers FAIR findability/interoperability/reusability, while Gilani2025 (CMEO, 50+ cardiovascular studies) finds generic registry standards 'lack formal semantic relationships necessary for variable-level alignment across studies.' The conflict maps squarely onto this subsection yet is absent. (Lower-confidence than [16]/[11] because the section never mentions ISO/IEC 11179; the writer may waive with a documented scope reason.)
findings.evidence: Package conflict [7]: paper_a Stotl2025 'ISO/IEC 11179 ... automatically serve to make data adhere to FAIR data principles'; paper_b Gilani2025 'ISO/IEC 11179 ... lacks formal semantic relationships necessary for variable-level alignment.' resolution_status open.
findings.suggested_fix: Either cite Gilani2025 to reinforce the fidelity-gap claim (and Stotl2025 as the optimistic counter-claim being rebutted), or record a one-line waiver that ISO/IEC 11179 metadata registries are outside the ontology/CDM scope of this subsection.

findings.location: Section 'Preclinical animal data at the back of the queue' -> ELN paragraph
findings.claim_text: Electronic laboratory notebooks are advocated across chemistry, computational drug discovery, and regulated bioanalysis as the route from analogue records to FAIR-aligned capture at source (Solle2020, HerresPawlis2022, Higgins2022).
findings.issue: The sentence explicitly names three ELN domains, but the three attached citations cover chemistry (HerresPawlis2022) and general/academic lab data capture (Solle2020, Higgins2022) - none is the 'computational drug discovery' or 'regulated bioanalysis' paper. Both named domains have dedicated package papers that are uncited: Schaduangrat2020 (ELNs in computational drug discovery/cheminformatics) and Zeng2011 (ELN in a GLP/regulated bioanalytical laboratory).
findings.evidence: Schaduangrat2020 finding: 'In computational drug discovery, electronic laboratory notebooks are increasingly replacing paper records...'. Zeng2011 finding: 'A well-designed ELN implemented in a GLP/regulated bioanalytical lab improved efficiency... and regulatory compliance...'.
findings.suggested_fix: Attach Schaduangrat2020 to 'computational drug discovery' and Zeng2011 to 'regulated bioanalysis' (e.g. '...chemistry (HerresPawlis2022), computational drug discovery (Schaduangrat2020), and regulated bioanalysis (Zeng2011)...'), or narrow the list of named domains to those the current citations support.

findings.location: Multiple (declared-vs-actual gap; policy paragraph; interoperability; retention; qualitative-harm)
findings.claim_text: Cited keys Hamilton2022, Gabelica2022, Smith2007, Colavizza2024, Prosser2024 carry consequential claims (0.3% / OR 9.5; 6.8% / same-rate; ontology interoperability; 4.3% citation advantage; qualitative-mandate harm).
findings.issue: Provenance/verification gap: these five section-cited keys have NO finding in evidence_section_04.json (they exist only in the citemap and, for four of them, in conflict verbatims). Their claims are therefore not backed by a curated verbatim source sentence in the package. Four are recoverable from conflict paper_claim verbatims (Hamilton2022 OR 9.5 = conflict [8]; Gabelica2022 same-rate = conflict [8]; Smith2007 ontology = conflict [9]; Colavizza2024 4.3% = conflict [14]; Prosser2024 harm = conflict [10]); Gabelica2022's 6.8% figure was externally confirmed by this critic (123/1792). Hamilton2022's 0.3% is the erroneous one (see MUST_FIX Track 2).
findings.evidence: extract_cite_keys(section) shows these 5 keys cited; none appears as a finding.doi/finding.cite_key in the package. External check: Gabelica2022 abstract 'only 123 (6.8%) provided the requested data' out of 1,792 who promised.
findings.suggested_fix: Add curated package findings (with verbatim source sentences) for these 5 papers so the audit trail is complete; at minimum flag them for Phase 16 full-text verification. No prose change required for the four conflict-backed claims.

findings.location: Section 'Shared is not reusable' and figure fig-sec4-fair-reusability
findings.claim_text: a dental-research corpus averaged 2.4 out of 10 on Reusability (Uribe2022) ... urban air-quality datasets ... returned Reusable scores of 2 to 3 out of 10, with Interoperability the weakest dimension (Syed2025).
findings.issue: The specific numeric reusability sub-scores (Uribe 2.4/10; Syed 2-3/10) are not present in the package source sentences for these papers. Uribe2022's package verbatim documents only '200 of 7,509 articles stated they had data'; Syed2025's verbatim states 'reduced FAIR Interoperability and Reusability scores... particularly where machine-readable standards were absent' but gives no numeric /10 value and names both Interoperability AND Reusability as reduced (prose singles out Interoperability as weakest). Values are plausible from each paper's own reporting but unverifiable from the package.
findings.evidence: Uribe2022 finding source sentence: 'the text-mining algorithms indicated that 200 items were indexed by stating that they had data.' Syed2025 finding: 'These issues align with reduced FAIR Interoperability and Reusability scores... particularly where machine-readable standards were absent.'
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm the 2.4/10 and 2-3/10 figures against full text in Phase 16; keep the figure-caption caveats (already noting n=112 / n=4 and different tools).

findings.claim_text: in global-health data reuse, upstream cleaning and curation consume the great majority of analyst time before any analysis begins (Waithira2026).
findings.issue: Scope: the package source sentence is a single interviewee's quote ('A geospatial analyst... described spending 80% of their time curating data'). The prose generalizes one anecdote into a field-wide 'great majority of analyst time' claim.
findings.evidence: Waithira2026 finding: 'A geospatial analyst working in Laos, Myanmar and Thailand described spending 80% of their time curating data before they could start analysing it.'
findings.suggested_fix: Qualify as illustrative, e.g. 'one analyst described spending 80% of their time on curation before analysis (Waithira2026)', rather than stating it as a general rate.

findings.claim_text: Package conflict [15]: Schmeiss2026 (altruism dominates data-sharing willingness) vs Kim2026a (personal benefit is the largest driver).
findings.issue: This package conflict is entirely absent from the section (neither side cited). It concerns participants'/donors' MOTIVATIONS to share genomic data (financial vs altruistic), which is a recruitment/consent question rather than the data-stewardship/FAIR-delivery argument the section makes. Flagged for completeness; judged legitimately out of the section's scope rather than a genuine suppression.
findings.evidence: Package conflict [15], resolution_status open. Neither Schmeiss2026 nor Kim2026a appears in the section; both are classified WAIVED_OUT_OF_SCOPE in coverage_review.
findings.suggested_fix: No action required beyond an explicit scope note; if the coordinator disagrees, a one-line acknowledgment could be added where incentives (Woods2022) are discussed.

findings.claim_text: roughly 8% of medical papers declared their data were publicly available while only about 2% actually shared them, with public code sharing below half a percent (Hamilton2023).
findings.issue: The 'public code sharing below half a percent' clause is not in the package source sentence, which reports only the 8% declared / 2% actual data figures.
findings.evidence: Hamilton2023 finding source sentence covers only 'declared and actual public data availability of 8%... and 2%... between 2016 and 2021.'
findings.suggested_fix: Verify the code-sharing figure against full text (plausibly reported by the same meta-analysis).

findings.location: Section 'Findability and access are unevenly delivered'
findings.claim_text: ORCID coverage differs substantially between institutions and data sources, and is not yet sufficient for automated reporting (Schnieders2022, Vrabel2016).
findings.issue: Vrabel2016 supports only the general ORCID-identifier concept (resolving name ambiguity, linking outputs); the specific 'coverage differs / not sufficient for automated reporting' claim is Schnieders2022's. Mild over-attribution in the compound cite.
findings.evidence: Vrabel2016 finding: 'ORCID... assigns persistent unique identifiers that automatically link to a researcher's publications...'. Schnieders2022 carries the coverage-insufficiency finding.
findings.suggested_fix: Attribute the insufficiency claim to Schnieders2022 alone, or keep Vrabel2016 only for the ORCID-definition clause.

findings.location: Section 'Findability and access are unevenly delivered'
findings.claim_text: matching only about 36% of taxonomic names to publications across three databases (Page2023).
findings.issue: Package effect size is '36% of names for which publication data are available'; the prose slightly widens this to '36% of taxonomic names', implying a share of all names.
findings.evidence: Page2023 effect_size source sentence: 'This represents approximately 36% of names for which publication data are available.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add 'of names for which publication data exist' to preserve the paper's denominator.

findings.location: Section 'Is universal retention worth its cost?'
findings.claim_text: a 122,000-publication analysis found that depositing data in a repository was associated with only a 4.3% citation advantage on average, and none for sharing code (Colavizza2024).
findings.issue: Only the '4.3%' figure is verbatim in the package (conflict [14]). 'none for sharing code' and the '122,000-publication' sample size are not in the available verbatim (Colavizza2024 has no package finding).
findings.evidence: Conflict [14] paper_b Colavizza2024: 'sharing data in an online repository correlates with a smaller yet still positive citation advantage of 4.3% (+/-.8) on average.' (no code/sample-size text).
findings.suggested_fix: Verify the code and sample-size claims against full text (Phase 16); consider a package finding for Colavizza2024.

findings.location: Section 'Is universal retention worth its cost?'
findings.claim_text: roughly 85% of community-curated databases have lifespans under fifteen years, with peaks in database loss tracking five-year funding cycles (Dowding2026).
findings.issue: The '~85% under 15 years' figure is in the package verbatim; the 'peaks in database loss tracking five-year funding cycles' detail is not in the available source sentence.
findings.evidence: Dowding2026 source sentence: 'approximately 85% of all community-curated databases have lifespans of less than 15 years.'
findings.suggested_fix: Verify the funding-cycle claim against full text.

findings.location: Section 'Shared is not reusable' (GEO omics sentence)
findings.claim_text: only 11.5% shared all of their important phenotype metadata while 37.9% shared less than 40% ... roughly a quarter of critical metadata omitted on average (Huang2025b).
findings.issue: The '11.5% / 37.9%' figures are verbatim in the package only under Huang2021 (the bioRxiv preprint; conflict [12] paper_a), not under Huang2025b, which the section cites. Huang2025b's own verbatim gives '74.8% shared / over a quarter omitted'. Almost certainly the same GEO study (preprint vs Genome Biology version), so benign - but the exact numbers are traced to the preprint key.
findings.evidence: Conflict [12] paper_a (Huang2021): 'Only 11.5% of studies completely shared all phenotypes, while 37.9% shared less than 40%.' Huang2025b finding: 'studies often omit over a quarter of crucial metadata, with an average of only 74.8% shared.'
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm 11.5%/37.9% are in the published Huang2025b; if only in the preprint, cite accordingly or use the published figures.

findings.claim_text: only 1.5% of 7,509 dental research articles shared data at all (Uribe2022).
findings.issue: The package verbatim says 200 of 7,509 dental articles (2.7%) STATED they had data; 1.5% (~112) is the smaller subset that actually shared/was FAIR-assessed (per the figure caption n=112). Stated-vs-shared distinction is blurred.
findings.evidence: Uribe2022 finding: '200 items were indexed by stating that they had data' (200/7509 = 2.66%); figure caption uses n=112 for the shared corpus (112/7509 = 1.49%).
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify '1.5% actually shared data (vs 2.7% that merely stated data existed)'.

findings.location: Section 'The governance qualifier: FAIR reuse versus CARE'
findings.claim_text: emerging equitable global-health frameworks explicitly reject a default 'open' setting in favour of governed access (Mayor2026, Calac2026).
findings.issue: Mayor2026 directly supports 'reject default open in favour of governed access'. Calac2026 is about using implementation-science frameworks (CFIR/ERIC) to design digital-health tech respecting Indigenous priorities - topically adjacent but does not itself state a rejection of default-open access.
findings.evidence: Calac2026 finding: 'an implementation science framework might guide the design of emerging digital health technologies best respecting the interests and priorities of Indigenous Peoples.'
findings.suggested_fix: Attribute the 'reject default open' claim to Mayor2026 (and West2026/Carroll2022b); use Calac2026 for the design-respecting-Indigenous-priorities point.
